FDW-16-2024

IN THE COURT OF KING’S BENCH OF NEW BRUNSWICK

FAMILY DIVISION

JUDICIAL DISTRICT OF WOODSTOCK

Citation: 2024 NBKB 224 ‘cor’

Date: 20240919

BETWEEN:

MINISTER
OF SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT

Applicant

– and –

D.A.L. and K.D.G.H.

Respondents

DECISION

BEFORE:

Justice Cameron Gunn

AT:

Woodstock, New Brunswick

DATE OF HEARING:

September 9-13, 17-19, and October 4 (Written Submissions) 2024

DATE OF DECISION:

October 29, 2024

APPEARANCES:

I. Mae Florina, on behalf of the Applicant.

Jonathan Martin, on behalf of the Respondent K.D.G.H.

LA Henry and Catherine McLatchie, on behalf of M.D.L.H. (the
child)

CORRIGENDUM:
Two instances of
the inclusion of the name of a party have been removed from the original and
replaced with initials. Corrigendum issued November 19, 2024

INTRODUCTION
AND OVERVIEW

1
.

M.D.L.H.
[1]
is 15 years old and her
early life was spent in Ontario with the Respondents, D.A.L. and K.D.G.H who are
her parents
.
[2]

Those years were not always happy ones and her parent’s relationship was, for
some significant period of time, one of conflict.

2
.

At
some point D.A.L., her mother, removed M.D.L.H. from Ontario and relocated to
New Brunswick. This was without her father’s consent or knowledge. He initiated
a search for M.D.L.H. which led to her discovery in this province and a subsequent
request for assistance by the Ontario child protection authorities to their New
Brunswick colleagues.

3
.

As
a result of the above request and subsequent investigation, the Applicant, the Minister
of Social Development (the “Minister”) placed M.D.L.H. in protective care on
July 29, 2022
[3]
.
She has been continuously in that care since then, a period of 27 months. The Minister
now seeks a guardianship order for
M.D.L.H
pursuant
to
s. 69(1)
of the
Child and Youth Well-Being

Act
,
S.N.B. 2022, c. 35 (the
Act
).

4
.

D.A.L.
participated in early proceedings but has taken no part in the guardianship
application despite being served. K.D.G.H., on the other hand, has been an
active participant. He opposes the Minister’s application. He has also filed an
application seeking relief under the
Divorce Act
and the
Family Law
Act
and by order of the Court on September 29, 2023, his application was,
pursuant to Rule 6.01 of the Rules of Court, ordered to be heard consecutively
with this matter so that evidence in one matter would be the evidence in the
other.

5
.

M.D.L.H.
had counsel appointed to represent her interest

in the Application.
She
has expressed her desire that guardianship be ordered.

This
decision is about whether guardianship will be ordered.

THE POSITION OF THE PARTIES

6
.

The
positions of those involved are as follows:

a)

The

Minister seeks guardianship for the reasons described
under the heading Minister’s position.

b)

K.D.G.H.

requests that the guardianship application be
dismissed with solicitor-client costs and a parenting order be made in his
favour. Alternatively, should the application be granted, he still seeks cost
on the basis of the conduct of the Minister. Finally, regardless of the outcome
he seeks reunification therapy for a period of 6 months, to be guided by named
experts.

c)

D.A.L.

took no part in the

Minister 's application despite being served
.

d)

M.D.L.H.
supports the application for guardianship.

ISSUES

7
.

The

issues

in

this

matter
are
:

a)

Is
it in
M.D.L.H.’s

best interests to grant the guardianship order sought
by the Minister pursuant to
s. 69(1)
of the
Act
?

b)

Alternatively,
is it in the child’s best interests to reunite
K.D.G.H.

and M.D.L.H. and, if so, in what manner?;

c)

If
guardianship is ordered, should the Court order reunification therapy or some
other form of post-guardianship contact? and

d)

Should
K.D.G.H. be awarded costs regardless of the outcome?

PRELIMINARY ISSUES

8
.

This
was a long and sometimes difficult hearing. The matter was originally scheduled
for 5 days but the evidentiary portion of the hearing actually lasted 8 ½ days
with the parties, at their request, filing written submissions at a later date
(which I find was the end of the hearing). During the course of proceedings, a
number of legal issues arose which required decisions which I delivered during
the course of the proceedings with reasons. I begin these reasons with an
explanation of those issues, the decisions I made and the reasons for them. I
do this, in part, as some were of a type, not ordinarily part of a hearing of
this nature.

Challenges
to the Experts

9
.

Both
the Minister and the Respondent K.D.G.H. sought to call experts who were
challenged, by the other party on partiality. In both cases I found the experts
were properly qualified and allowed them to provide opinion evidence. While I
rendered decisions in the trial, as I was required to do, I provide the
following brief comments on the admissibility of expert opinion evidence and
why I allowed it in over the objection of the opposing party.

10
.

Counsel
for
K.D.G.H.
raised two preliminary objections to
the testimony of Dr. Barbara Jo Fidler. The first was that the Notice to Call
Expert Witness filed by the Minister was deficient in that it did not disclose
what opinion she would express. There was some irony in this objection as
counsel for K.D.G.H. was deficient in his obligations having filed and provided
a notice of expert only two business days before trial and nearly one month
after a date fixed for such notice in a Procedural Order of the Court.

11
.

Counsel
for the Minister noted that the essence of Dr. Fidler’s testimony was contained
in her reports and the Minister sought to call her to provide information and
education to the Court on the issues of parental alienation and multi-faceted
family therapy (for parent child contact problems).

12
.

The

Act
contemplates that an application, including an application for
guardianship, shall be made in accordance with the Rules of Court
[4]

and that “to the extent that they are not inconsistent with the provisions of
this Act, the Rules of Court apply to proceedings commenced” under the
Act.
[5]

13
.

The

Act

contains no specific requirement for expert reports. The Rules of
Court, on the other hand, specifically address notice regarding experts. Rule
52.01(1) reads:

52.01Condition Precedent to Calling
Expert Witness at Trial

a)

(1)
Where a party intends to call an expert witness at trial, he shall serve on
every other party a copy of the expert’s signed report which shall contain, or
be accompanied by, a statement containing the expert’s name, address and
qualifications and the substance of his proposed testimony. Service shall be
made as soon as practicable and no later than the Motions Day at which the
trial date is fixed.

14
.

The
Rule does not require the Notice to detail an opinion, but rather contain a
copy of the expert’s signed report which shall contain, or be accompanied by, a
statement containing the expert’s name, address and qualifications and
the
substance of his proposed testimony
. I found that the notice of the
Minister was sufficient, and I dismissed this objection.

15
.

The
second objection was that
the witness could not be
qualified as she was not impartial having been retained as a consultant by the
Minister.  K.D.G.H.  did not otherwise oppose Dr. Fidler as unqualified.
Counsel for the Child consented to Dr. Fidler’s qualifications. I dismissed
this objection to Dr. Fidler’s qualifications from the bench. My reasons for
doing so are detailed here.

16
.

Properly
used, expert opinion evidence provides judges with information and knowledge
they would not otherwise possess. It also, however, has the danger of
overwhelming the trier and obscuring the role of the judge. To balance the
benefits and risks the Supreme Court of Canada has developed (and modified) the
criteria for the admissibility of expert opinion evidence.

17
.

In

R. v. Mohan
[6]
,

the Court established the eponymous threshold requirements for admissibility:
(1)
relevance, (2) necessity, (3) the absence of other exclusionary rules; and (4)
proper qualification.

18
.

A
criticism of the
Mohan
criteria was that they did not lead to easy
application, a concern that Doherty J. of the Court of Appeal for Ontario
sought to rectify
in
R. v. Abbey
[7]
.
He proposed a two-step process where the party proffering the evidence
demonstrates the existence of preconditions of admissibility at the first stage
and the trial judge exercises a gatekeeping function to determine whether the
preconditions to admissibility are sufficiently beneficial toward admission
despite the potential harm to the trial process.
[8]

19
.

This
two-stage analysis was largely adopted by
the Supreme Court of Canada in

White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and
Haliburton Co
.
[
White Burgess
]
[9]
. In that case the court
articulated test as follows:

Stage
one: are the threshold preconditions to admissibility met?

•
Is the proposed evidence logically relevant to a fact in issue?

•
Is the proposed evidence necessary?

•

Is
the proposed evidence otherwise admissible (i.e., there is no other
exclusionary rule)?

•
Is the expert properly qualified?

•
(If the science is novel or contested) Is the underlying novel science
reliable? (this is sometimes treated as an intermediate inquiry)

Stage two: do the potential benefits of admitting the
evidence justify the risks in doing so?

• Is the proposed evidence “sufficiently beneficial to
the trial process to warrant its admission despite the potential harm to the
trial process that may flow” from its admission?
[10]

20
.

Part
of the threshold analysis is a requirement that the proposed expert fulfil
their duty to the court by providing evidence that is
fair,
objective and non-partisan, to be aware of the duty and be able and willing to
carry it out.
[11]

If the threshold is not met, the evidence should not
be admitted. If it is met, “concerns about an expert witness’s independence or
impartiality should be considered as part of the overall weighing of the costs
and benefits of admitting the evidence.”
[12]

The threshold requirement is “not particularly onerous”
[13]

21
.

The Court held that “it is the nature and
extent of the interest or connection with the litigation or a party thereto
which matters, not the mere fact of the interest or connection.”
[14]
A mere employment
relationship with the party calling the evidence will likely not disqualify the
witness, but a direct financial interest in the outcome of the litigation
likely would. Likewise, an expert who assumes the role of an advocate for a
party is unable to carry out their primary duty to the court.
[15]

22
.

I considered the partiality question both
at the threshold stage and the cost-benefit stage. Dr. Fidler expressed a
willingness to meet her duty of impartiality, the fact that she was retained
did not disqualify her and I found that her evidence was admissible.

23
.

K.D.G.H. also called an expert witness,
Shawn Wygant, who is a forensic limited licensed psychologist in the state of
Michigan.
The Minister objected to his qualification alleging he
was not impartial. He had been a litigant against a foster care worker and the
child protection agency in his state for issues directly related to the opinion
he proposed to proffer. He had also offered preliminary opinions before being
provided complete materials.

24
.

As with Dr. Fidler, I was satisfied, at
both the threshold stage and the cost-benefit analysis stage, that the witness
was able to meet his duty to the court. The mere fact that an expert has been
enmeshed in unrelated legal proceedings that arise from a similar factual
matrix does not rise to the level of disqualification. If there was evidence
that the proposed expert was an advocate for the party or for a particular cause,
then I might have acceded to the Minister’s objection. The materials presented
on the
voir dire
, and the cross-examination of Mr. Wygant, did not
establish such a position.

25
.

As to the Minister’s second concern, that
Mr. Wygant had expressed opinions without complete information this, in my
view, was a matter that goes to the weight rather than admissibility.

Disclosure of Psychologist’s Notes

26
.

During the course of the testimony of Ms.
Lise D’Anjou Phillipe, a Psychologist and Psychological Parenting Capacity
Assessor, counsel for the Respondent began to cross examine her using materials
she had provided to Mr. Wygant, including raw data from personality tests
performed on the Respondent and her clinical notes from her session with the
Respondent.

27
.

The Minister initially objected to the use
of the raw data which I overruled. When it became apparent that counsel for
K.D.G.H. had also been provided clinical notes from the session with the Child
by Mr. Wygant, Counsel for the Child objected. The Minister joined in this
objection on the basis that the notes were privileged and confidential and that
the Minister, despite retaining the witness, was not able to have her notes.

28
.

Counsel for the Respondent suggested that
Counsel for the Child had no standing to object. This is not an accurate
statement of the law. As the Court of Appeal has noted:

Once legal counsel has been
appointed for a child, he or she has the right to fully participate in any
process that affects the child. This means the right to receive full
disclosure, the right to examine and cross-examine witnesses and the right to
participate in legal arguments, including the right to place the views and
preferences of the child before the court.
[16]

29
.

In a
voir dire
to determine the use
to which the raw data and notes could be put, Ms. D’Anjou Phillipe said that
she was not allowed to disclose the materials, except to another psychologist,
by virtue of her professional responsibilities. She had disclosed them to Mr.
Wygant within this context with the understanding they would not be otherwise
shared.

30
.

The witness is a member of the College of
Psychologists of New Brunswick, a self-regulated body established by
The
Psychologists Act
(2017).
[17]
That

Act
provides that the College may make regulations governing standards
for the practice of psychologists, the creation of a code of ethics or conduct
for psychologists and standards respecting the duties, tasks, services and
functions that form part of the practice of psychology.

31
.

Pursuant to its power the College has
adopted a Code of Conduct. That Code contains specific provision obligating
members to protect the security of tests.  it reads:

III.4.1.
The psychologist shall protect the security of tests.  To this end, members
must distinguish between test data and test materials.  According to the Personal
Health Information Privacy and Access Act (PHIPA), client health information,
which includes raw data from standardized psychological tests, must be released
to clients and others with proper authorization upon request (refer to PHIPA
for requirements and exceptions).  When possible, raw data should be presented
in summary form, rather than presented on testing material or protocols, and
efforts should be made to transfer the requested information to a qualified
professional.

III.4.2
Testing material is protected by copyright laws.  Because federal or provincial
legislation may require psychologists to release the content of files to
clients or others with proper authorization, testing material (such as test
questions, manuals, and protocols) should be excluded as much as possible from
the client files.  Testing materials contained within the client file should be
released to clients with proper authorization when ordered by a court or as may
be required under application federal or provincial legislation.
[18]

32
.

The
Code clearly makes provision for, and indeed creates an obligation to, release
to clients and others with proper authorization, raw data from standardized
psychological tests. In this case the client (in the context of his interview) was
the Respondent and he provided authorization to release raw data to Shawn
Wygant. There being no other restriction on the release of the data I found its
use was permitted.

33
.

With
respect to the clinical notes, this is also governed by the Code of Conduct.
Section III.2.1 obligates a psychologist to safeguard confidential information
obtained in the course of practice and, subject to certain exceptions, disclose
confidential information to others only with the informed written consent of
the clients. One of the exceptions to the general rule of confidentiality
allows the psychologist to share client information with other appropriate
professionals concerning the welfare of the client. This is subject to informed
consent from the client, when possible, in writing, when the sharing of the
information would enable the identification of the client.

34
.

In
this case Ms. D’Anjou Phillipe did not obtain such consent from the child. This
was because the Code of Conduct adopts the

Medical
Consent of Minors Act
[19]

as determinant of the age for informed consent. That
Act

establishes the
age of consent as 16 years or older.
[20]

35
.

Ms.
D’Anjou Phillipe was in this case, however, gathering information specifically
for the purposes of decisions to be made under the
Act
.
Section 22

reads:

22(1)
All information acquired by the Minister or any other person in relation to any
person or matter under this
Act
, whether of a documentary nature or otherwise,
is confidential to the extent that its release would tend to reveal personal
information, as defined in the Right to Information and Protection of Privacy
Act, about a person identifiable from the release of the information.

22(2)
The Minister may disclose confidential information referred to in subsection
(1) with the written consent of

(a) the
parent of the child, in the case of a child who is under 12 years of age, or

(b) the
child or youth, in the case of a child or youth who is 12 years of age or over.

22(3) A
person, other than the Minister, shall not disclose confidential information
referred to in subsection (1) without the written consent of the person from
whom the information was obtained and the person to whom the information
relates.

36
.

The
clinical notes in this case included personal information as defined in the
Act
.

As the child was over the age of 12 at the time of both the gathering of
the information and its disclosure, written consent was required for release.
It was not obtained. This is understandable as Ms. D’Anjou Phillipe believed
that she was governed by a Code of Conduct which would not allow for the
written consent of the child (who was under 16) and was unaware of the
provisions of the
Act
. Notwithstanding that, her actions were contrary
to the provisions of the
Act.

37
.

Given
this I held that “further questions about the contents of the notes, that is
the contents of the notes are not permitted, though if Dr Wygant is to testify,
and he requires the content of the note to form his opinion…he may talk about
how the content of the note  helped him form his opinion, not about the
specific contents of the note, subject to a further
voir dire
if Mr.
Martin wishes”.

38
.

On the following day counsel for the Respondent,
asked that I revisit my ruling relying on the general inclusionary rule and on Rule
60.03 of the Rules of Court to support his request.

39
.

With respect to
Rule
60.03,
he relied upon,
West v. Wilbur
.
[21]
That case makes it
clear, however, that Rule 60.03 relates to a judgement which has been given
after disposition of a motion.
In
West v. Wilbur
Justice McNally noted that
formal judgement had not been entered in that case and Rule 60.03 had no
application. The same is true here.

40
.

This did not foreclose, however, a
re-examination of my ruling on an evidentiary issue. Counsel can apply at any
time during the course of the trial for a judge to reconsider an evidentiary
ruling and indeed my original ruling invited such an opportunity.

41
.

As indicated above counsel relied on the
general inclusionary rule which states that the manner in which evidence is
obtained, no matter how improper or illegal, is not an impediment to its
admission at common law.
[22]

42
.

In
Chandra v CBC
,
[23]
Mew, J.  adopted the
rationale for the general inclusionary rule from Sopinka, Lederman & Bryant
at §9.3 which states:

The
trier of fact should have the benefit of all relevant evidence, irrespective of
how it was obtained. If illegal or improper acts committed in the acquisition
of evidence do not affect its probative value, they should not distract the court
from its primary task of fact finding.
[24]

43
.

The law is one of general inclusion and
not absolute inclusion and
in
Grech v. Scherrer
,
[25]
McKelvey, J. noted:

There may, however, be some limits
to the general inclusionary rule, where policy and societal considerations
outweigh the probative value of the evidence, even in a civil matter. The case
law does not appear well developed in this area.
[26]

44
.

Walker J,
in
McDermott v. McDermott
,
[27]
:

Recently,
however, where evidence has been obtained unlawfully or surreptitiously, courts
have recognized that there is a limited discretion at common law to exclude
relevant non-privileged evidence, the exercise of which involves “a balancing
of competing interests which can be usefully viewed as assessing the probative
value of the evidence as against its prejudicial effect”
[28]

45
.

Cases provided by counsel for the
Respondent fell into one of three categories: 1) cases that rely on the excerpt
from the
Law of Evidence in Canada
; 2) cases where evidence was
illegally obtained by police and the court found that the admission of evidence
in a criminal proceeding (or lack of such admission) had no impact on a civil
proceeding; and 3) cases were claims of privilege were defeated on the basis of
inadvertent disclosure.

46
.

It is worthy of note that no New Brunswick
cases were quoted, and I am unaware of any that have adopted the general
inclusionary rule. Even if they did, it is apparent that the cases recognize
that there is no absolute rule of inclusion or exclusion for evidence that has
been obtained in a manner that is illegal, contrary to a privilege, or barred
by statute. It is also worthy of note that the cases quoted relate to actions
other than child protection matters.

47
.

The provisions of part three of the
Act
,
which includes
ss. 22
-
23
,

appears clearly guided by a policy decision of
the legislature to ensure the confidentiality of information relating to
children. It is a recognition of the impact that public proceedings may have on
the health, development and well-being of people in their most vulnerable state.

48
.

Counsel correctly pointed out that the
provision does not relate to the admissibility of evidence but rather the
confidentiality of information. Notwithstanding this, evidence obtained in
violation of the provision can clearly be excluded if it’s inclusion would
defeat the purposes of the section. To find otherwise would be to ignore the
exception described above. That is that any general inclusionary rule, if one
is recognized in this jurisdiction, is still subject to limitations including
policy and societal considerations which outweigh the probative value of the
evidence.

49
.

As I had indicated in my original ruling,
the purpose of obtaining the notes was for use by an expert hired by the Respondent
to evaluate questions of parental alienation and appropriateness of treatment
regimes. It was also meant to allow for a challenge to the views of the psychologist
from whom the notes were obtained. She indicated that she was aware of this
when she provided the notes. The purpose of the hearing in which we were
engaged was to determine what is in the best interests of the child. As
noted
in
Chandra v CBC
there is a benefit to hearing all relevant evidence,
irrespective of how it was obtained. That said, the best interest the child
also includes respecting her privacy and autonomy. In my view both were able to
be achieved.

50
.

My original ruling, that the expert hired
by the Respondent could use the notes in supporting his opinion stood, but I
clarified it. I held that if Mr. Wygant was permitted to testify as an expert
witness (leave had not yet been granted to due to the lateness and deficiency
of the Notice of Expert), he would be permitted, in explaining the contents of
his report, both in direct and cross-examination, to refer to specific materials
in the notes that he has relied upon to form his opinion. His reference to
specific portions of the notes was limited to the requirement noted and he was
not to be permitted to testify generally as to the contents of the notes. Any
testimony about the contents of the notes was subject to my power to protect
the confidentiality of proceedings pursuant to
s. 134
of the
Act
.
Counsel for the Child and the Minister were provided the notes and encouraged
to use their knowledge of them to ameliorate concerns with respect to their
contents.

51
.

Ultimately, Mr. Wygant made no specific
reference to the notes during his testimony.

Can Counsel for the Child
Call a Witness

52
.

Counsel
for the Child advised that they wished to call a witness, specifically M.L. who
is the son of D.A.L. and the half-brother of the child. Counsel for the Child
indicated that the wishes of M.D.L.H., the child, were clear. She has
communicated to the Minister, to counselors, and to this Court through her
counsel, that she wishes the Guardianship Order to issue and does not wish to
be reunified with the Respondent K.D.G.H.

53
.

As
Counsel for the Child noted, the obvious position of K.D.G.H. is that the
wishes of the child are not based upon legitimate life experiences with the
Respondent but fostered by false information provided to the child by the
Respondent D.A.L. leading to alienation.

54
.

Counsel
for the Child indicated that the evidence of M.L. would provide corroboration
for M.D.L.H.’s well-founded fear of returning to the care of K.D.G.H. Specifically,
she expected M.L. to testify about K.D.G.H.’s aggressive, violent, and
controlling behavior as a parent.

55
.

Counsel
for the Respondent K.D.G.H.  opposed the motion on the following basis:

a)

That,
even if Counsel for the Child has a general right to call evidence, the
proposed evidence exceeded the statutory role of Counsel for the Child and
amounted to “tag teaming” by the Minister and Counsel for the Child against the
Respondent.

b)

that
the proposed evidence created procedural and substantive unfairness such that
it was contrary to the administration of justice. Specifically, he suggested
that allowing Counsel for the Child to call evidence that was effectively the
evidence of the Minister circumvented the Minister’s responsibilities for
disclosure and allowed such evidence to be called after the Respondent has
closed its case, thus effectively disabling him from meeting the evidence.

c)

that
he was taken by surprise in that he had been provided no indication of the
content of the testimony of M.L.

56
.

Counsel
for the Minister supported the motion and indicated that it had been the
intention of the Minister to call M.L. until they were advised by Counsel for
the Child that they were intending to call him. They then deferred to Counsel
for the Child.

57
.

When
confronted with the disclosure and procedural concerns counsel for the Minister
indicated that at the December 2022 hearing it was the intention of the Minister
to call M.L. and a will-say statement was provided at that time but that the proceeding
was resolved by consent. Counsel for the Respondent confirmed that he received the
will-say at that time but has not seen it since.

58
.

The
role of Counsel for the Child is defined in
s. 129
of the
Act
. It reads
as follows:

Role of counsel

129 Counsel
representing a child or youth in a proceeding under this
Act
shall:

(a) meet the child
or youth in advance of the proceeding without the parents present,

(b) speak with the
child or youth with respect to the issues and explain the available options, to
the extent that it is appropriate, based on the child or youth’s age and
maturity,

(c) listen to the
views and preferences of the child or youth, if the child or youth is able to
express them, based on the child or youth’s age and maturity,

(d) communicate to
the Court the views and preferences of the child or youth on their behalf,
including the extent to which and the method by which the child or youth wishes
to participate in the proceedings, and

(e) make
submissions to the Court based on the views and preferences of the child or
youth.

59
.

Counsel
for the Child pointed to authority that suggests that the role of counsel to
the child is not restricted to communicating to the court the wishes of the
child but that they play an active role in the testing of evidence, making
representations to the court and ensuring the rights of the child are
respected.

60
.

The
role of counsel for the child has been a controversial one. In
Child
Representation in Alberta: Role and Responsibilities of Counsel for the Child
in Family Proceedings
, the authors state:

While there is
some variation in terminology, commentators have generally identified three
possible roles for counsel appointed to represent a child: the friend of the
court, the best interest’s guardian, and the child's advocate.
[29]

61
.

In

S.H. v. Minister of Social Development and C.H
.
[30]

the Court of Appeal considered the role of the Counsel for the Child. This was
in the context of a guardianship application in which the trial judge ordered
guardianship for five children be awarded to the Minister against the opposition
of the child's mother. One of the grounds of appeal was that the judge erred
when she did not address the divergence between the children’s views and
preferences and the “position” taken by counsel for the children.

62
.

The
Court of Appeal noted that International Convention and the Supreme Court of

Hearsay
Evidence

83
.

Another issue was the receipt of hearsay
evidence.

84
.

For judges and lawyers more comfortable in
a purely adversarial system, such as criminal courts, the frequency of hearsay in
child protection matters can be jarring. That is not to say, however, that it
is legally impermissible or inappropriate.

85
.

Justice Bourque recently discussed the
issue
in
MSD
v. J.L. and J.F.
[46]

and wrote:

[16]
A substantial amount of evidence presented by the Minister in this matter
consisted of statements made by the child to third parties (social workers,
teachers, and other school staff) regarding abuse he suffered at the hands of
his father. It is important to note that counsel for father did not object to
or challenge the admissibility of these out of court statements and for that
reason it was not necessary to conduct a voir dire. I do however feel compelled
to address the subject of admissibility since several of the child’s out of
court statements will be referred to throughout my dissertation of the facts.

[17]
Hearsay consists of an out of court statement offered to prove the truth of its
content. Unless the statement falls under one of the exceptions in the common
law or the evidence is admitted pursuant to the principled approach, hearsay is
not admissible.

[18]
Hearsay statements made by a child will often not satisfy the common law
exceptions to the hearsay rule. However, there are times when the child’s
hearsay evidence is the best evidence of the issue being litigated. For this
reason, courts have adopted “a much more benign attitude to children’s
evidence” (see: R. v. B. (G.) [1990] S.R.R. 30).

[19]
Our Court of Appeal recently addressed the issue of hearsay statements in child
protection matters in its decision of
M.V. and C.H. v.
Minister of Social Development,
2021 NBCA 42
.  At paragraph 31, the Court
referred to the distinction between civil and criminal proceedings when it came
to applying the hearsay rule:

Professor
David Paciocco, as he then was, in an article entitled "The Principled Use
of Hearsay in Civil Cases: A Technical Guide to Avoiding Technicality"
(2008) 87:2 Can. Bar. Rev. 277, recognized the distinction between criminal and
civil cases in the application of the principled exception. In his view:

Perhaps the most
telling reason for lessening the intensity of the hearsay rule in child
protection matters is that the proceedings are less adversarial and more
inquisitorial.

86
.

Since
the Court of Appeal’s
decision in
M.V.
and C.H. v.
Minister of Social Development,
[47]
the
legislature has created
the
Act
which now governs child
protection. In doing so it has recognized the unique nature of child protection
hearings.
Section 60(8)
of the
Act
which is part of the section on procedures
on the hearing of applications reads:

60(8) During a hearing, if a person
introduces hearsay evidence, the Court shall receive the hearsay evidence and
shall determine whether the evidence received is reliable and the weight to be
given to the evidence in the circumstances.

87
.

This
legislative provision essentially codifies an obligation to receive hearsay but
then determine its value. No specific guidance is offered on how reliability
and weight are to be assessed.

88
.

Section
132 also provides a permissive authority to receive the evidence of a child or
youth through hearsay. Its admissibility is determined by one of the parties
(not the Court)
determining it is necessary.
[48]
The
Court is assigned the task of determining its reliability depending on the “child
or youth’s age, maturity, credibility and ability to communicate and the weight
to be given to the evidence in the circumstances.”
[49]

89
.

Finally,
s. 133 allows for the admission of hearsay of a person other than a child in a
number of enumerated ways. Again, admissibility is determined by one of the
parties (not the Court) determining it is necessary.
[50]
Though there is no specific
requirement to assess weight or determine reliability, it is apparent for a
reading of the entire
Act
in context and the jurisprudence of our Court
of Appeal and the Supreme Court of Canada
[51]
that
a reliability assessment is required.

90
.

While
a child protection hearing has been described as a
quasi-inquisitorial proceeding
[52]
accurate fact-finding remains
necessary for a fair determination of what is in the best interests of the
child.  While the traditional “gatekeeper” function of the trial judge on
admissibility may have been legislatively circumscribed, the proper adjudicative
function still requires an assessment of reliability.

91
.

Given

Credibility

96
.

Credibility forms an important part of my
assessment of the best interests of M.D.L.H.  in this case. From the outset of
the matter, the Respondent suggested that he wished the lead social workers,
Heidi Baird and Jennifer Bennett, excluded as their credibility was an issue.
The credibility of every witness is, of course, at issue, including that of the
Respondent.

97
.

The assessment of credibility in the
context of family law shares similar characteristics to and criminal law and
other areas of civil law. Wooder, J. in
A(A) v. B(M)
,
[57]
provided
guidance on the topic and wrote that assessing credibility is “a sifting of
nuances, impressions and observations impacted by such things as a witness’
demeanour, tone and candor, as well as the context of his or her evidence.”
[58]

98
.

Credibility is not simply an exercise in
determining the veracity of a witness’s evidence, but also its reliability. A
perfectly truthful witness may nonetheless be incredible because they lack the
capacity to observe, recount and recall what they have seen, heard or otherwise
experienced. It is important in assessing credibility to consider both the
veracity of the witness, that is their willingness to tell the truth as they
know it, and the reliability of the witness.

99
.

Credibility is also not an all or nothing
matter.

The judge may believe some, none, or all of the evidence given by a witness.

[59]

100
.

There is no magic formula for the
assessment of credibility but factors that courts have found to be relevant
are:

a)

External consistency: the consistency of
the testimony with other independent evidence that has been accepted.
[60]

b)

Internal consistency:  Inconsistencies in
testimony, between trial testimony and prior statements, or between two or more
prior statements can all assist in the assessment of veracity.
[61]

c)

A Motive to Lie
or

Tell the Truth: if a witness has an interest in the outcome of a trial that is
a relevant factor “
among others, to take into account
when assessing the credibility of the witness’s testimony”.
[62]

d)

The
Opportunity to Observe or Perceive: Perception or observation can be enhanced
or impeded by internal and external factors like the nature of the event and
distance, duration, and location of observation.

e)

The
Capacity to Observe or Perceive: The circumstances of the observation and the
observer can both impact capacity. Age, impairment, and physical state, amongst
other things, can impact capacity.

f)

The
Capacity to Communicate Observations and Perceptions: Memory, intellectual and
physical impairments can be important to the capacity to communicate.

g)

The Witness’s Character for Truthfulness:
When a witness testifies their “character for truthfulness or mendacity is
relevant circumstantial evidence on the question of the truthfulness of the
witness' testimony.”
[63]

h)

Testimonial Demeanour:
testimonial
demeanour has been described as "every visible or audible form of
self-expression manifested by a witness whether fixed or variable, voluntary or
involuntary, simple or complex".
[64]

It remains a relevant, but controversial, criteria for assessment and caution
is warranted as assessments based on demeanour “are no substitute for those
based on a critical analysis of the substance of the entire evidence.”
[65]

i)

Plausibility or
Reasonableness
of the Account: Whether the story harmonizes with the preponderance of the
probabilities which a practical and informed person would readily recognize as
reasonable in that place and in those conditions is a useful factor in
assessing credibility.
[66]

101
.

As
noted above, while testimonial demeanour remains a consideration in credibility
assessments, it is one I view with extreme caution. For over half a century,
appellate courts have recognized its dangers.
In
Faryna v. Chorny
, the
British Columbia Court of Appeal held that sole reliance on it to determine credibility
can reward good acting rather than actual sincerity and can produce an
arbitrary finding.”
[67]

102
.

Appearances
of telling the truth do not equate to credibility and appellate courts have
noted “a growing understanding of the fallibility of evaluating credibility
based on the demeanour of witnesses.”
[68]

103
.

Using
demeanour as a factor in assessing credibility “risks applying amateur
psychology because their manner of giving evidence may reflect matters
unrelated to credibility, including personality, culture, or the impact of
testifying about a traumatic event.
”
[69]

104
.

Assessing credibility in child protection
cases has an added nuance. Much of the evidence produced is by affidavit. As
the Court of Appeal has noted, “matters of credibility cannot be resolved
on affidavit evidence alone.”
[70]
Indeed,
some judges have specifically declined to make credibility findings on the
basis of  untested affidavit evidence.
[71]
Of
course, a judge may find the contents of an affidavit to be incredible, and may
use the contents of an affidavit, supplemented by oral testimony, to determine
the credibility of a witness.
[72]

I am mindful of these restrictions in this case.

105
.

Based upon the breadth of the information

.

.

rather likes the word “efficacy”. She measures efficacy as progress against

.

335
.

Guardianship
applications are governed by the
Child and Youth Well-Being Act
,
[122]

(the “
Act
).
Section 59
empowers the Minister to apply for a guardianship
order if the Minister has reason to believe that the well-being of a child or
youth is in danger.

336
.

Section 34 defines the circumstances under
which a child may be in danger. In this case the Minister suggests that it has
such grounds on the following basis:

(e) the
child or youth is being or is at substantial risk of being neglected or
ill-treated as a result of being in the care of a person who fails to

(i)
provide adequate food, clothing or shelter,

(ii)
provide adequate affection or respond to the cues of the child or youth or the
need for cognitive stimulation, or

(iii)
seek appropriate medical, surgical, dental, mental health, remedial care or
rehabilitative treatment for the child or youth or consent to the care or
treatment,

(f) the
child or youth is being or is at substantial risk of being neglected or
ill-treated as a result of being in the care of a person who fails to ensure
the child or youth attends school or follows an approved educational plan and
who has failed to comply with subsection 15(6) of the Education Act;

(h) the child
or youth is being or is at substantial risk of being psychologically or
emotionally harmed;

(j) the child
or youth is living in an unfit, unsafe or improper environment;

(l) the
parent or person having responsibility for the child or youth fails or is
unable to protect the child or youth from harm; or

(n) the child
or youth has suffered multiple incidents of harm or patterns of behaviour that
result in harm.

337
.

The

Court

has

jurisdiction

to make

a
G
uardianship
O
rder

pursuant
to
s. 69(1)
of the

Act

which
provides as follows:

69(1) The Court
may make a guardianship order transferring from a parent to the Minister, on a
permanent basis, the guardianship of a child or youth, including the custody,
care and supervision of the child or youth and all other parental rights and
responsibilities with respect to the child or youth.

338
.

The

Act

is clear that in making any decision
that affects a child or youth under the
Act
that this Court is obligated
to
consider the best interests of the child above all other
considerations.
[123]

339
.

The

best

interest

of

the

child

criteria is certainly not a new creation of the
Act
.
It existed in the predecessor to the current legislation and is common to
similar legislation in other provinces and related federal legislation. Our
Court of Appeal has clearly directed that the best interest of the child is

the “sole test used
to determine child custody”
[124]
and
that the
best

interests
must

be

examined from

the

standpoint of the

child

and

not

from

the

standpoint

of the

parents.
[125]

340
.

The
approach to the assessment is to be contextual and fact specific. A
“case-by-case consideration of the unique circumstances of each child is the
hallmark of the process”
[126]

guided by the individual factors described in the governing legislation. Those
factors, which will be addressed below, have no primacy amongst them and the
“evidence that lays the foundation for the factors must first itself undergo a
discretionary determination by the judge, regarding its admissibility,
credibility, reliability, and weight.”
[127]

341
.

The
burden of proof is, as in all civil matters, on a balance of probabilities.
[128]
Conclusions
on whether that standard has been met may be settled on credibility
assessments.
[129]

342
.

The
statutory factors to be considered are set out in s. 5(2) and are:

(a) the child or
youth’s physical, mental and emotional development and needs, the ability and
willingness of the parents to meet those needs and the care or treatment
required to meet those needs,

(b)
the importance of family to the security and well-being of the child or youth
and family as the preferred environment for the care and upbringing of children
and youth,

(c)
the child or youth’s cultural, linguistic, religious, and spiritual upbringing
and heritage, including Indigenous upbringing and heritage,

(d) the child or
youth’s sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression,

(e) the importance
of the child or youth’s stability, continuity of care and familial
relationships, including with immediate family, and the possible effect of any
disruption in that continuity,

(f) the importance
of permanency to the security and well-being of the child or youth,

(g) any family
violence and its impact on the child or youth, including whether the child or
youth is directly or indirectly exposed to the violence,

(h) the child or
youth’s views and preferences as provided for in section 6,

(i) the impact on
the child or youth if there is a delay in taking action or making a decision,
and

(j) the nature and
impact of past parenting practices that endangered the well-being of the child
or youth.

343
.

As
part of a review of the best interests of the child, the role of the Minister
and any interventions is relevant. A court is “required to undertake a review
of the various interventions made by Ministerial representatives as a matter of
context”
[130]

including “a review of Case Plans that were implemented, and the expert reports
that were prepared.”
[131]

It is not the role of a judge in the best interest analysis to defer or
delegate the decision to the Minister. It is the job of the court to conduct
its own analysis.
[132]

may grant me the power to make such orders as are necessary to achieve the
legislative objectives and discharge my burden. I need not do so here as I find
that the Order that is in the best interests of the child is one that I have
specific power to make. Reunification, immediate or on gradual basis, is not in
the best interest of
M.D.L.H.

The Application of the Respondent

426
.

As noted above, the
K.D.G.H.’s

application was consolidated with this one, with the
intention that it be heard consecutively. Considering all of the evidence and
the legislation as described above,
K.D.G.H. ‘s application
is denied. The evidence is the same as in the guardianship application, and the
only thing that differs is the burden.

427
.

In
making my decision I have clearly considered K.D.G.H.’s arguments in opposition
to guardianship and his capacity to meet the needs of M.D.L.H. I was still
convinced that the Minister had met its burden. As such, I am clearly not
satisfied that K.D.G.H. has met his burden and his application is not granted.

Costs

428
.

The
Respondent has asked that I award costs. The Minister has been successful in
its application. Despite this, I am prohibited from ordering costs against the
Respondent.
[142]

429
.

As
for the Respondent’s request, despite the assertions of counsel I have found
the activities of the Minister to be in accordance with its obligations under
the
Act
. I decline to order costs as requested.

Post
Guardianship Reunification

430
.

K.D.G.H.
has requested that if I order guardianship, I order that reunification therapy
continue. While specific in its nature, this is a request for post-guardianship
access.

431
.

Since
the creation of the
Act

judges of this Court have wrestled with the
issue of whether a judge of the Court of King’s Bench has jurisdiction to order
post-guardianship access under the
Act.

432
.

Some
have noted absence of legislative authority providing discretion to order
post-guardianship contact and the presence of specific authority for the
Minister to grant permission for the same in
s. 69(5)
of the
Act
.
[143]

433
.

Others
have held the Court retains jurisdiction to order post-guardianship access
under
s. 5(1)
of the
Act
.
[144]

434
.

I
accept, adopting the analysis of Justice Daigle in
Minister of Social
Development v. C.G.,
that I retain jurisdiction to grant post-guardianship
access. I decline, however, to order. The child has clearly expressed her
desires and they include discontinuing any access with K.D.G.H. She is clearly
negatively affected, at present, by efforts to move her toward increased
contact. Based upon my best interest of the child analysis I find that it would
not be in the best interest of M.D.L.H. to order post-guardianship access.

435
.

This
does not preclude, of course, the Minister from exercising the power in
s.
69(5)
.

436
.

69(1) of the
Act
,

the

Minister is
granted guardianship
of M.D.L.H.
